title: Razor in Green
subtitle: A razor, impeccably sharp and dressed in green, that stands up for the people.

content.text: *breath in* *breath out* O-oh, you're here? Not a good time. As you can see, my eyes are barely open.
*sighs* In the blink of an eye, my dream slips away like a deer into the deep of the forest.
Were you dreaming?

branch.text: Heh, what kind of question is that? You make it sound like me dreaming is the most ridiculous thing in the world!
I have to remind you, except for some out-dated wisdom, there is nothing different between your head and mine, dearie.

content.text: What did you dream of?

branch.text: I'm as curious about that as you are.
You could always allow me to return to my soft bed to try to summon that dream again. But even then, it likely won't be the same dream.
See, we seldom remember our dreams, and even what we don't forget can be hard to understand. And that's why we need a dream interpreter.
A doctor that values Shakespeare above his patients, and cigars above his own career—a doctor like Sigmund Freud.
He lures out forgotten memories from your past, through a technique called "free association." Through this, he can reveal what makes you who you are.
All you need to do is to lie on the sofa, and spill out your thoughts like old milk.

Once you do that, your mental health will surely improve. The sleepwalkers stop falling out of their beds, the hysterical go back to their sewing, with enough time maybe Nietzsche could write a comedy.
"But what about the medical journals?" You may ask. He must have released them. Otherwise, how could we prove the effectiveness of his treatments?
And he has. You can read them in journals, in the text books, and hear them in the chattering of medical students—
Your name will be blacked out on the pages by then, but your dreams will become the latest gossip on everyone's lips.

content.text: It's not good for the patients.

branch.text: Oh my dear, all medicine has side effects. The best medicine is bitter to the taste.
It must be tolerated for the sake of the treatment. How else will these patients free themselves from their mental cages of unconscious desire and delusion?
It really is the smallest of prices—a mere coffee stain on your shirt, just telling a few people about an unlucky moment or two.
Besides, the patient does not give a name. The true protagonist remains a secret between you and the doctor.
Heh. Perhaps you're right. It's not the only way ...

content.text: What's the other, then?

branch.text: Come, listen ... Do you hear that? That shrill, piercing sound of metal on the skull, the blood-cuddling screams ... Even the strongest soul would quake in fear.
But this is the other way. However, funny enough, some people prefer the pain. It ends faster than a hard talk with the doctor.

content.text: Hey, you! Yes, you, my hurried child, you rush through the street like a cyclone ... Where are you going?
I can't be late for the show!

branch.text: A show, a show! So you came to Vienna for the love of stories. That's for sure.
Then this is just the right place for you. A place where the floors are decorated with gold, where music sings along with the stories ... Even a newcomer could be entranced here.
Oh, listen to me! You must not be a newcomer, but a true connoisseur! Well, before you leave, may I ask a simple question?
Which act in a show do you prefer?

content.text: Act One.

branch.text: Oh! Well begun is half done! You're always right to the point. We should know how a story starts and when we have stepped onto the path of fate.

content.text: Act Three.

branch.text: Haha! The rising action! The most thrilling part, like biting into the filling of an apple strudel—you're about to have the sweetest part!

content.text: Act Five.

branch.text: Yes, of course! The resolution, coming to its fated ending. We stand up and cheer, or stay in our seats and weep ... Our reward for not falling asleep during the intermission, worth every krone you've paid.

content.text: Every part of it.

branch.text: Haha, so greedy. It's a tough choice, isn't it? But you can't escape from making decisions.

content.text: Do you know which act I love the most? Not Act One, nor Three or Five ...
But Six. Oh! Act Six, my dear, that's the best part.

The part in which the king picks up his fallen head; the knight pulls out the sword in his chest; the bodies stand up, dust their clothes and come to the front of the stage, bow to the audience and receive their applause ...
That's not really a part of the performance ...

branch.text: Yes, it is! My child, that is precisely when the real show begins.
I have a good script here. Let me put on my glasses ... Hmm ... Let's start from ... from Act Six.
The princess, a nightingale decorated with diamonds, an opera singer taking center stage, steps into a building of gray-and-white diamond patterns.
"And the curtain falls forever. The smile on her face seems too serene. She is still dreaming."
"Her madness keeps them all alert. But in the court, she seems so meek and mentally steady, like a docked boat on calm waters."
"Nodding elegantly to every gentleman she meets, she makes the shackle on her neck look like a piece of dazzling jewelry."
Next page ... oh.

content.text: What happened?

branch.text: "In a transparent room, under an unyielding limelight, her dignity is stomped on, like a silk handkerchief thrown on the ground. They smash her crown, forcing her to pay for her madness."

content.text: Is she mad?

branch.text: No ... not anymore.
"'Sleep, she said to me, sleep. If that's what she said, then I don't need to wake up.'"

"That's when the star falls into an ever-lasting dream. The blinding light becoming a spotlight on the stage; the empty room carrying the best reverberations. She has never been so calm. Everything beautiful in her is there forever, frozen in time."

content.text: I guess she went completely insane.

branch.text: Or found eternal peace.
"Her world has become the performance. A show that never ends."
I'll say she's a great actress, isn't she?

content.text: But this is not a good story. I think it needs more context.

branch.text: Hahaha, my dear. You are indeed a great connoisseur.
Only one act of a play can't tell a good story by itself.
Oh, forgive my ramblings. The golden curtain has risen.
Fix your collar, darling, and keep moving forward.

items.text: E lucevan le stelle
Razor in Green
Ladies and gentlemen, welcome.
Meeting Hall

items.speaker: Dr. Schwartz
items.text: On behalf of the General Medical Association of Vienna, I would like to thank you all for attending this demonstration conference.

items.speaker: Dr. Schwartz
items.text: It is a great honor!

items.speaker: Dr. Schwartz
items.text: As we can see, dear friends, the era of science has arrived, THE ERA OF MAN HAS ARRIVED! Today, we will share the honor of witnessing the advancement of technology, its contributions to medical science and even the world.

items.speaker: Dr. Schwartz
items.text: Now please allow me to introduce the patient again: Ms. Isolde von Dittarsdorf. This lady has selflessly volunteered for the experiment, and in return will receive a healthy mind in no time.

items.speaker: Dr. Schwartz
items.text: She's been living a miserable life due to hysteria. How terrible it is for a young woman like her.

items.speaker: Dr. Schwartz
items.text: As we all know, mental illness is taking an increasing toll on our country. Even suicide has become more rampant.

items.speaker: Dr. Schwartz
items.text: The tragedies are piling up, and our dear lady is in excruciating pain as we speak!

items.speaker: Dr. Schwartz
items.text: Thanks to the development of medical science, we can again be rescued from the abyss of pain. As I said before, the electroshock therapy uses the most advanced technology available.

items.speaker: Dr. Schwartz
items.text: The medical use of electricity dates back to the 18th century ...

The presentation of these obscure theories fails to enthrall the attention of the guests. Vienna's citizens possess less a thirst for knowledge than a hunger for morbid curiosities. Tales of misfortune are favored over their cures.

items.speaker: Citizen I
items.text: Isolde?

items.speaker: Citizen I
items.text: The youngest daughter of the Dittarsdorfs?

items.speaker: Citizen I
items.text: Oh, no wonder she volunteered. The treatment should do wonders for her!

items.speaker: Citizen I
items.text: You know there's something wrong with that family ... I heard her mother stabbed old Dittarsdorf in the temple with a brass needle and killed every maid in the room.

items.speaker: Citizen I
items.text: That thing's even made it into the curio market. I heard not even the Lourdes water could clean the blood off it.

items.speaker: Citizen II
items.text: The family seems to be cursed. So far, no one's ever lived past the age of 40. In fact, the girl had a sister who died very young. And now her brother—I read in the papers that ...

items.speaker: Citizen I
items.text: He killed himself, right?

items.speaker: Citizen II
items.text: Well, the artist did what an artist would do. He wrote a sad poem, and then set fire to his paintings, together with himself.

items.speaker: Citizen I
items.text: You know what, my uncle works for the police, he showed me the autopsy report. The truth is, Theophil shot himself! He was killed by a bullet ...

items.speaker: Citizen III
items.text: Gosh! Good thing he didn't have to suffer all that pain before he died ... Poor boy, he was so talented and handsome!

items.speaker: Citizen III
items.text: But the girl, oh, she's less fortunate! Fainted at her only brother's funeral, didn't even get to see him one last time ... I hope the latest treatment will alleviate her suffering ...

items.speaker: Citizen II
items.text: Lunatics, the whole family is a bunch of lunatics!

items.speaker: Citizen I
items.text: Manners, sir! This is Vienna, where we call these poor people ... "arcanists."

items.speaker: Citizen III
items.text: *sighs* I sincerely hope that Isolde can put an end to her miserable nightmare. After all, she is one of the most talented opera singers in Vienna, just like her mother.

items.speaker: Citizen I
items.text: You know what they say, talent and hysteria go hand in hand. Think about it, they both come from the mind!

items.speaker: Citizens
items.text: Hah!
The speaker notes these untimely whispers.

items.speaker: Dr. Schwartz
items.text: Quiet please. The treatment will now begin.

items.speaker: Dr. Schwartz
items.text: Are you ready, Ms. Dittarsdorf?

items.speaker: Isolde
items.text: Y-Yes.

items.speaker: Isolde
items.text: *deep breath*

items.speaker: Isolde
items.text: I'm ready. Please ...

items.speaker: Isolde
items.text: Uggh!!

items.speaker: Dr. Schwartz
items.text: Three, two, one, okay. Calm down, my lady. Just hang in there, okay? The treatment will work.

items.speaker: Dr. Schwartz
items.text: Perseverance is a virtue. I don't think the electric shock is causing the pain you seem to be experiencing. Don't let the imaginary fear get the better of you.

items.speaker: Isolde
items.text: Ugh ... Ugh ...

items.speaker: Isolde
items.text: Yes ... Sir ...

items.speaker: Dr. Schwartz
items.text: Good.

items.speaker: Dr. Schwartz
items.text: Now we'll begin stage two. The voltage will be slightly increased.

items.speaker: Dr. Schwartz
items.text: Please get ready, Ms. Dittarsdorf.

items.speaker: Isolde
items.text: Ugh ... Ugh ... I-I ...

items.speaker: Isolde
items.text: Ahh! No, no ...

items.speaker: Dr. Schwartz
items.text: Stage three, an even higher voltage ...

items.speaker: Isolde
items.text: Ugh!!! Ahhh!

items.speaker: Isolde
items.text: All other sound has faded away.
Enough!
Forgive the interruption, Dr. Schwartz, but I need you to stop the treatment immediately!
Chattering, hushed questions replace the hum of electricity. The audience turns toward the petite woman standing in the back row.
I can't help but to question your methods, as well as the methods of the General Medical Association.

items.speaker: Isolde
items.text: *pants*
Your electroshock therapy is a gross violation of humanitarian principles. Judging from what I just saw, it only brought the patient meaningless pain, and didn't help her condition one bit.
Unless, of course, you intend to use physical pain to distract the patient from her mental pain?
Her green silhouette is delicate and sharp, like a razor slicing through the chaos.

items.speaker: Dr. Schwartz
items.text: Even though this is a conference meant for conversation, you're being ... a little rude.

items.speaker: Dr. Schwartz
items.text: The new electroshock therapy is not what you know from the last century. Now that man has tamed electricity, there's no doubt that the EST is the best choice for treatment! You shouldn't take it at face value, because it's not like the underlying principles are the same as that frog experiment, heh.

items.speaker: Dr. Schwartz
items.text: My treatment is supported by systematic theories and reliable references, and it is approved and sponsored by the General Medical Association, which means it's reasonable and legitimate.

items.speaker: Dr. Schwartz
items.text: While you are, correct me if I'm wrong, a "social activist" known for her little arcane tricks. Ms. Kakania, or should I say, Ms. Klara.

items.speaker: Dr. Schwartz
items.text: As far as I know, you don't even have a medical degree. Besides, your so-called art movement, the "Secession," is it? It confuses me, really.

items.speaker: Dr. Schwartz
items.text: Anyway, in order to have a more professional conversation, I suggest we talk later, you know, after you get a medical license!
Murmurs and fragmented laughter swell among the crowd.

items.speaker: Kakania
items.text: No, Dr. Schwartz. This conversation has nothing to do with my personal identity or experience. I'm only asking you as a citizen of Vienna, and as a "human being" with empathy!

items.speaker: Kakania
items.text: How can you not see that she's suffering? Have you been thoroughly brainwashed by the supposed authority of medical science, or have you too been blinded and deafened by hysteria?

items.speaker: Dr. Schwartz
items.text: You rude little ...!

items.speaker: Dr. Schwartz
items.text: Please allow me to reiterate: the EST is an advanced and reliable treatment! Besides, Ms. Dittarsdorf had signed an agreement before we started. The experiment is conducted under mutual consent.

items.speaker: Dr. Schwartz
items.text: Your objection is of no use, and is even harmful to the patient's interests.

items.speaker: Dr. Schwartz
items.text: But we always welcome debate. Since you question my methods, please, be my guest and indulge us with your thoughts on her condition.

items.speaker: Kakania
items.text: As I understand it, Mr. Sigmund Freud published his Studies on Hysteria in 1895.

items.speaker: Kakania
items.text: He believed that hysteria was a psychological disorder caused by problems in the nervous system. It was not a simple organ disease.

items.speaker: Kakania
items.text: His Trauma Theory explained that the patient's personal life experiences were the real causes of the disorder, affecting the patient in subtle ways.

items.speaker: Kakania
items.text: It makes much more sense to analyze the patient's traumas than to harm their body.

items.speaker: Kakania
items.text: As to whether his theory is "advanced" enough, you can read the Totem and Taboo, which he published last year ...

items.speaker: Dr. Schwartz
items.text: ... What?!
The gentleman's face cracks with expression.

items.speaker: Dr. Schwartz
items.text: Freud ... Freud?!

items.speaker: Dr. Schwartz
items.text: The man who told people to marry their mothers and kill their fathers?! The one who couldn't get a word in when his patient spewed her insanity?

items.speaker: Dr. Schwartz
items.text: It took him 17 years to become a professor, for God's sake!

items.speaker: Dr. Schwartz
items.text: Ms. Klara, I've tolerated your immature antics, and I always welcome advice and opinion, as long as they're rational and reasonable. It's just ... how could you challenge me with such an amateurish theory?

items.speaker: Dr. Schwartz
items.text: You insult me as a gentleman! And you insult my reputation!

items.speaker: Kakania
items.text: What? Dr. Schwartz, I did not mean to insult you ...
*bang—*

items.speaker: Citizen III
items.text: Ah!

items.speaker: Citizen III
items.text: Ms. Dittarsdorf, she's unconscious!

items.speaker: Dr. Schwartz
items.text: ... How?

items.speaker: Kakania
items.text: Get her off the chair! Now!
TO BE CONTINUED…
